final_recommendation: The room converged on a narrow labor-enforcement amendment via December 2019 Protocol: Mexico delivers labor code documentation Wednesday, all three countries sign Friday a protocol with automatic 15% tariff triggers (10-day activation post-inspection), trilateral inspection calendar locked at launch (no unilateral Mexico postponement), and explicit firewall against reopening dairy/autos/Chapter 19. Congress commits to January 2020 ratification vote contingent on that exact language. The deal collapsed on incompatible public messaging frames—Congress cannot simultaneously claim 'we forced Mexico's hand' to labor/business and allow Mexico to tell its domestic audience 'we kept full commission voice'—but the substantive terms were locked.
minority_objections: Mexico's sovereignty concern that U.S. controls inspection schedule unilaterally (resolved via trilateral commission structure but messaging tension remains)
Canada's insistence that any amendment be labor-only with explicit firewall against dairy/autos reopening (accepted but required repeated written guarantees)
key_conflicts: Incompatible public messaging frames: Congress telling labor 'automatic tariffs, no Mexico veto' vs. Mexico telling domestic audience 'trilateral commission with full voice'—trade_lawyer and media_actor identified this as fatal to trust

Mexico's sovereignty red line (inspection scheduling control) vs. Congress's enforcement red line (no Mexico veto on inspections)—resolved via trilateral commission but created messaging vulnerability
Canada's firewall demand (labor-only amendment) vs. implicit risk that any text reopening invites broader renegotiation
key_concessions: Mexico accepted automatic tariff triggers with zero discretion and trilateral inspection calendar it cannot unilaterally postpone
Congress accepted trilateral commission structure (not U.S. unilateral enforcement) to preserve Mexico's sovereignty narrative
Canada accepted a formal amendment to USMCA text (not just standalone protocol) provided it explicitly firewalls labor-only changes
Business lobby accepted two-week timeline uncertainty in exchange for locked enforcement numbers and January vote commitment
red_lines: Congress: automatic tariff activation within 10 days post-inspection with no 'pending review' escape hatch—anything less kills caucus votes
Mexico: trilateral commission retains scheduling voice (not U.S. unilateral control)—losing this kills domestic political cover
Canada: amendment must be labor-only with explicit exclusion of dairy, autos, Chapter 19 renegotiation—any broader reopening is non-starter
Labor union: independent inspections on locked 12-month calendar Mexico cannot unilaterally delay—postponement authority read as veto
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: The incompatible messaging frames (enforcement win vs. trilateral balance) were identified by trade_lawyer and media_actor in R6 but never resolved—both Congress and Mexico committed to Friday public statements that contradict each other
No mechanism specified for what happens if the first press question Friday exposes the messaging contradiction and one government walks back its commitment

Canada's written guarantee (R6) removes Canadian uncertainty but adds pressure on Mexico to finalize—no discussion of what Canada does if Mexico's Friday protocol language differs from Wednesday's labor code docs
Business lobby's mobilization timeline (immediate support upon Friday signing) assumes messaging alignment that does not exist
downstream_risk_variables: Whether Mexico's Friday protocol language actually says 'automatic tariffs activate 10 days post-inspection' with zero discretion or includes sovereignty-preserving qualifiers that Congress reads as escape hatches

Whether Congress's Friday public statement emphasizes 'we forced automatic enforcement' or 'trilateral commission with Mexico voice'—the former satisfies labor/business, the latter satisfies Mexico, both cannot coexist
Whether Canada's explicit firewall language in the amendment survives legal review or creates loopholes for future renegotiation claims
Whether Mexico's domestic political cover (trilateral commission narrative) survives if U.S. media coverage frames the deal as 'Congress forced Mexico to accept automatic tariffs'
Whether the January 2020 ratification vote timeline holds if the messaging contradiction surfaces in Friday's press coverage and erodes trust on either side
uncertainty_notes: The substantive enforcement terms converged (automatic tariffs, trilateral calendar, labor-only amendment, January vote), but the public messaging frames remain incompatible and unresolved. Congress committed to telling labor/business 'we forced automatic tariffs with no Mexico veto' while Mexico committed to telling its domestic audience 'we secured trilateral commission voice, not U.S. unilateral enforcement.' Trade_lawyer and media_actor identified this contradiction as fatal to trust in R6, but no participant proposed a unified messaging strategy before the Friday signing deadline. The deal's survival depends on whether both governments can sustain contradictory domestic narratives without the first press question collapsing one side's political cover.

marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Drove every round: R1 'package as signed doesn't have the votes', R4 'selling my caucus a political win that collapses in court', R5 'my votes evaporate' if Mexico can delay inspections—ratification failure was the central threat forcing all concessions
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_pressure: Dominated R1-R5: labor_union demanded '30-day inspection cycles, 15% tariff suspension within 10 days, union-busting resolved in 60 days' (R1), Congress required 'automatic trigger with zero discretion' (R4-R5), shaped entire protocol structure
marker_evidence.business_lobby_support: Present but secondary: R1 'business mobilizes support today' if Mexico commits, R2 demanded 'concrete protocol by Friday', R6 conditioned support on public enforcement story—important but followed labor/Congress lead rather than driving
marker_evidence.canadian_domestic_acceptability: Persistent defensive concern: R1 'dairy's settled, won't renegotiate', R3-R6 repeated demands for explicit firewall against reopening dairy/autos—shaped amendment structure but did not drive the core labor enforcement negotiation
marker_evidence.mexico_labor_sovereignty_risk: Central tension throughout: R3 Mexico demanded 'no veto but we control our labor enforcement internally', R5-R6 insisted on 'trilateral commission with full voice' narrative—drove the trilateral structure compromise and created the unresolved messaging contradiction
marker_evidence.media_public_pressure: Consistent but supporting role: R1 'public narrative is USMCA lacks teeth', R6 'one of those stories dies in the first press question'—media_actor identified key risks (messaging contradiction) but did not drive the substantive terms
marker_evidence.agreement_stability: Drove the amendment path: R1 'reopen it or we're stuck', R3 trade_lawyer 'protocol floats free, you're exposed to legal challenge', R5-R6 all parties recognized the deal required formal amendment to survive ratification—stability contingent on amendment was the room's operating assumption from R1 forward
